## The Naive Fix Destroys the Risk {.center}

To carry uncertainty forward, you must **sample**.

. . .

The obvious move — sample each asset on its own — gets every marginal right and
the **joint catastrophically wrong**.

. . .

It can never produce the co-crash. And the co-crash is the risk.

## Independent Sampling Kills the Joint {auto-animate=true}

::: {#aa9fd8ec .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='11' execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=2144 height=703}
:::
:::


Identical marginals. Only joint generation keeps the co-crash.

## The Spine — The Same Machine, Backward

$$\underbrace{z = T(x)}_{\text{forward: measure / remove}}
\qquad
\underbrace{x = T^{-1}(z)}_{\text{backward: propagate}}$$

- A map that *simplifies* one way **generates** the other
- Draw $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, invert → a real, dependent scenario
- The change-of-variables formula is the recipe: $p_X(x) = p_Z(T(x))\,|\det J|$

## Uncertainty Is a Distribution, Not a Number {auto-animate=true}

::: {#6c1cdcec .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='8' execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1544 height=664}
:::
:::


A point forecast — or a thin Gaussian band — hides the loss that lands in the
tail it never represented.

## #2 Gaussian Monte-Carlo — Thin Tails {auto-animate=true}

Fit a covariance, sample a normal. Captures linear co-movement, but Gaussian
tails are **thin** and tail-*independent*.

::: {#4e98a874 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='11' execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=2143 height=623}
:::
:::


Same cloud in the middle, **too-optimistic VaR** at the edge.

## #3 RBIG Backward — Keeps the Real Tail

Learn $T$, sample in Gaussian space, invert. The same tool that measured
dependence (Module 1), now a **generator**.

::: {#8834b7e9 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='10' execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1943 height=662}
:::

## #4 The Other Uncertainty — Around a Prediction {.center}

So far we sampled the *joint* to price a portfolio. Now: the uncertainty around a
single **prediction** $\hat y = f(x)$.

. . .

Two different questions — two tools, no priors needed:

- **aleatoric** — *how noisy is the world here?* (data noise)
- **epistemic** — *have I even seen data here?* (model doubt)

## Tool A · Predict the Noise {auto-animate=true}

Fit the mean $f(x)$; the **residuals are the noise**. One error bar assumes that
noise is constant — it never is. So fit a *second* model to the squared residuals
→ $\sigma(x)$, and band with $f(x)\pm 2\sigma(x)$.

::: {#689a0b93 .cell fig-height='3.3' fig-width='11' execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=2143 height=604}
:::
:::


Same coverage — but the constant bar cries wolf in the calm zone. $\sigma(x)$ puts
the doubt where the world is actually noisy.

## Aleatoric Is Volatility {auto-animate=true}

In markets the noise has a name — **volatility** — and it is *predictable*: it
clusters. Forecast $\sigma_t$ from the recent past (EWMA) and band with
$\pm 2\sigma_t$.

::: {#70bc4ddc .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='11' execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=2138 height=624}
:::
:::


The band widens exactly when it must — yet still misses ~7% of days (it should
miss 5%): fat tails. Gaussianize the residuals to close the gap (Module 2).

## Tool B · Ensembles — Does the Model Know?

Refit on resampled data → an **ensemble**. Where the members *agree*, the model is
sure; where they *fan out*, it isn't — and that happens where it has seen no data.

::: {#47b77703 .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](03-uncertainty_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1743 height=624}
:::
:::


Epistemic uncertainty **balloons in the gap**. Add the two:
$\sigma_{\text{aleatoric}}(x)^2 + \sigma_{\text{epistemic}}(x)^2$.

. . .

*(A Bayesian net is the principled limit; a deep ensemble is the cheap, robust
stand-in — same answer, far less machinery.)*

**forward** → measure (M1) · remove (M4)    |    **backward** → propagate (M3)

## The Whole Course, One Line {.center}

> Claim only what your evidence justifies.

. . .

The Gaussian is the least-committal joint; what $T$ removes or generates is
*exactly* the dependence in the data.

. . .

**Signal, neutrality, and risk are one operation — read three ways.**
